title: Hurricane Lowell battered Hawaii’s western islands and is linked to at least 2 deaths
text: HONOLULU -- Hurricane Lowell’s intense winds and storm surge that battered Hawaii’s western islands this week are suspected in the deaths of at least two people. On the island of Kauai, the storm damaged oceanfront resorts while on Lanai, a cargo port where much of the island’s food and supplies arrive was inoperable, the state’s governor said. Lowell brushed by the islands in the overnight hours Tuesday with damaging winds that extended well beyond the hurricane’s centre, which stayed offshore. First responders on Kauai’s south end found the body of a 74-year-old man on Wednesday near the shoreline. Authorities believe his death was related to the storm surge, police said. Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said another man was killed on Oahu when a large tree fell on his tent Monday during the storm. The man was homeless and living in a park, he said. Green on Wednesday asked U.S. President Donald Trump to issue a major disaster declaration to expedite federal help for Kauai and Maui counties. Lowell has since been downgraded to a tropical storm and continues to move westward over open water. New storm forms in the Pacific Tropical Storm Norbert formed Thursday in the Pacific Ocean and wasn’t threatening land, forecasters said. The storm was about 685 miles (1,102 kilometres) southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula of Mexico, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said. It had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph (64 km/h) and was moving west. There were no coastal watches or warnings in effect, the centre said. Some gradual strengthening was forecast over the coming days.

title: Did you just see a mosquito? Here’s how the rain can extend mosquito season in Toronto
text: The amount of rain that Toronto has seen over the last week might cause mosquitoes to buzz through the city for longer than usual. Mosquito season typically lasts from May through September, with populations peaking in early June in southern Ontario before dropping rapidly after Labour Day. But some experts who spoke with CTV News this week say that the city appears to still be seeing a significant number of mosquitos, likely due in part to the wet start to September, including a massive storm on Sept. 2 that dumped more than 130 millimetres of rain on parts of the GTA. Toronto got another 10 to 20 millimetres of rain on Wednesday. “It is largely because of, well almost entirely because of that huge amount of rain that we’ve received,” Rosalind Murray, an assistant professor of biology at the University of Toronto Mississauga, told CTV News Toronto. One reason why there are more mosquitoes buzzing around Toronto, Murray says, is due to an “explosion” of floodwater mosquitoes. Dormant mosquito eggs can be activated when an area is flooded by water, Murray explained. Last week’s storm caused widespread flooding across Toronto, even resulting in an extended closure of Don Valley Parkway. “We can have these dormant eggs all of a sudden become living, breathing, active mosquitoes,” Murray said. Another reason there are more bloodsuckers around is due to the temperature, Murray noted, as there wasn’t a “crazy hot” summer this year and they tend to thrive in slightly cooler temperatures. Mosquitoes are at their most active when it is humid outside, she said, which is typically during dusk and dawn. “They don’t want to desiccate, they don’t want to dry out,” Murray said. “When it’s a bit cooler, when it’s overcast, the risk of desiccation is a lot lower and so you start to see them become more active during the day.” Coupled with lower temperatures, this leads to longer-lived mosquitoes. Garrett Brown, branch manager for Orkin Canada’s downtown Toronto location, told CTV News Toronto that he has seen a slight increase in calls for mosquitos this year but he said that has been somewhat offset by a later start to the season amid cooler spring temperatures. “I initially thought it would be more of a worse season because we had such a deep snowfall last winter,” Brown said. Amid the extended season, Brown recommends removing as much standing water as possible to prevent mosquitoes from breeding, like buckets, children’s toys, and frequently changing out the water in bird baths a couple of times a week. “Often, leaves will get in the roof gutters. I twill cause drainage problems and now you’ve created a source for the mosquitoes to breed in,” Brown said. The pest expert also advised keeping grass short and trimming shrubs frequently, so they don’t get overgrown. “They’re hiding inside those shrubs in shaded areas, so if you can trim those back, allow as much airflow and sunlight to get in, the better it will be,” he said. As soon as it gets colder in Toronto and freezing temperatures set in, Murray says the mosquitoes will disappear. “So, for now, in the immediate, acute mosquito season, it’s only going to be a few more weeks max, because they are ectothermic,” Murray said. “Any cold temperatures, as soon as we start seeing those really cold nights compared to the days that we get in the early autumn, then we should see a drastic decrease in the number of mosquitoes.”

images.caption: An image of a mosquito on a person's arm.

title: Girls worst hit by climate shocks on schools: UNICEF
text: Girls are at greater risk of dropping out of education when their schools are hit by heatwaves, storms or wildfires linked to climate change, the UN children’s agency said on Thursday. UNICEF analysis suggested that one in 10 or more than 171 million students in 106 countries or territories had their education disrupted by extreme weather last year. But the agency said girls were worst affected when schools were damaged, classes cancelled or education switched online. “Girls are at greater risk of dropping out when climate hazards disrupt or close schools,” it said. “Damage to schools and sanitation facilities, displacement and lost family income can place additional caregiving and water-collection responsibilities on girls. “These pressures can also increase the risk of child marriage, making it more difficult for girls to return to class when schools reopen.” According to the analysis, storms were the most common cause of disruption and last year affected 109 million students around the world. Floods hit at least 70 million while heatwaves disrupted schooling for some 50 million youngsters. The overall figures for 2025 are down on analysis of the previous year, in which UNICEF said nearly 250 million children in 85 countries -- one in seven -- were affected by climate hazards. The agency said it had changed its methodology, basing its analysis on information from aid agencies and local media rather than government figures. UNICEF said about one billion or about half the world’s children live in countries at very high risk of climate and environmental shocks. Lost learning and the effects on literacy and numeracy could lead to lifetime income losses of at least US$200 billion and worsen global inequalities, it estimated. Most of the children come from low- and lower-middle income countries “where education systems often lack the resources needed to safeguard learning during climate-related emergencies”, the study said. UNICEF urged governments and their partners to spend more on building new educational facilities to withstand climate and environmental hazards.

title: Toronto still responding to thousands of service requests in wake of ‘100-year storm’
text: Toronto is still responding to the thousands of service requests in the wake of the “100-year storm,” marking the largest storm-response the city says it has ever seen. In an update on Tuesday, the City of Toronto said it received nearly 5,700 storm-related service requests regarding damage from the torrential rain. Of those requests, more than 3,000 are related to impacted trees, the city says. This has pushed tree cleanup into this week. “Crews (have) been working extended hours to address the most urgent public safety concerns and restore access to critical infrastructure,” city officials wrote. “This work is prioritized with critical infrastructure and roads being top priority.” Last Wednesday’s walloping storm brought destructive winds and ping pong sized hail, knocking out power for thousands of homes across Toronto and flooding major roadways like the Don Valley Parkway. Some areas in the GTA saw more than 100 millimetres of rainfall, like Vaughan, Scarborough and North York. As of Tuesday, city officials said it has finished more than 1,000 service requests, including fully clearing expressways and arterial roads. The city says there is still work being done on removing road blockages on collectors and local roads. Toronto says it has also been supporting emergency response and critical infrastructure partners, like Toronto Hydro and the Toronto Transit Commission, so service can return to normal. The city says it has taken extra measures over the last week to tackle this added work, including extending shifts of specialized urban forestry crews and deploying more skilled surge capacity contractor crews to accelerate tree maintenance cleanup. It is unclear at this time when the city will finish this work.

title: Nepal glacier saw exceptional heat before collapse caused deadly floods: researcher
text: The mountain section whose collapse triggered fatal floods in Nepal and China on Aug. 26 had experienced unprecedented heat for the time of year, meteorological data analyzed by a researcher shows. Average temperatures on the mountain glacier at an altitude of 5,200 metres (17,060 feet) were estimated at around five degrees Celsius between Aug. 21 and 26. This is exceptionally high. They had not exceeded 4.0C over the same period in more than 55 years of data recording, although no direct link to the collapse has so far been established. This series of highly localized temperatures was reconstructed by Robert Rohde, chief scientist at the independent Berkeley Earth organization in California. At the site of the collapse, the average temperature recorded over that six-day period has risen by about 1.8C since the mid-20th century. Without the additional heat brought by climate change, a comparable temperature pattern “would probably occur only once in a few thousand years”, Rohde calculated for AFP. The collapse came during the Langtang region’s fourth-hottest summer on record, according to AFP’s analysis of data from Europe’s Copernicus observatory dating back to 1970. Tipping point “These hot conditions can also explain permafrost thaw and combined slope and glacier collapse,” said French climatologist Valerie Masson-Delmotte. Permafrost acts as ice cement, holding rock faces together. Its degradation makes them more unstable. Satellite images also showed significant snowmelt in the days before the disaster, providing “a substantial source of liquid water that can infiltrate fractures in the mountain and facilitate landslides”, said Etienne Berthier, a glaciologist at France’s CNRS research agency. Experts remain cautious, however, about the precise role played by the heatwave. “It’s not as straightforward as ‘high temperature equals collapse,’” Kristen Cook, a geomorphologist at the Grenoble Alpes University in France, told AFP. “If the temperature acted as a trigger, it seems that it needed to wait until the rock was right at the tipping point of collapse,” she added. Researchers are now examining the small movements observed in the mountain in the years before the collapse and their interaction with changes in temperature. “Proving the rock near the fracture plane was significantly weakened as a result of meltwater and/or permafrost thaw” would be a “smoking gun” of climate change, according to Rohde of Berkeley Earth. His temperature analysis used data from the Copernicus programme’s ERA5 climate model and a network of 14 high-altitude weather stations located between nine and 140 kilometres (six and 87 miles) from the collapsed glacier.
